item.title: The Surprising Power of Mindset for Depression
item.description:
Depression

The Surprising Power of Mindset for Depression

Our beliefs about emotions can shape recovery.

Posted October 22, 2026

Key points
  • People who believe their emotions are malleable tend to have fewer symptoms of depression.
  • Malleable beliefs lead people to use better strategies for dealing with their moods.
  • Telling people depression stems from a chemical imbalance may give them the wrong mindset.

You’ve probably heard about the power of mindset when it comes to education. As the developmental psychologist Carol Dweck famously showed, students with a growth mindset tend to do better in school than students with a fixed mindset because they're less likely to give up in the face of setbacks. What you might not know is that new research is showing mindset can have a powerful effect on dealing with negative emotions, or moods.

Source: Kindel Media/Pexels

Suppose you wake up after a poor night of sleep, groggy and irritable. Do you see your mood as malleable, something you can change with a little effort? Or do you see it as fixed, something beyond your control?

Psychologists call these “emotion malleability beliefs.” It turns out that people who believe their emotions are malleable tend to have a greater sense of well-being, fewer symptoms of depression, and more confidence in their ability to manage their emotions.

The reason is that people who think their emotions are malleable tend to use superior cognitive strategies to deal with their moods. One such strategy is “cognitive reappraisal,” the ability to take a different perspective on your mood.

If you wake up groggy and annoyed, you might think, “Well, one bad night of sleep probably won’t destroy my day." In contrast, people with more fixed beliefs tend to use inferior strategies, such as rumination, where you obsess over how bad life is. “Why does this keep happening to me?” is the refrain of those with fixed mindsets about emotions.

Can Mindset Impact Depression?

I talked with Elizabeth Kneeland, psychology professor at Amherst College and a leader in the field of emotion malleability and depression, to find out more. As she put it, “if you think your emotions are outside your control, will you cope with them differently? Are you at risk for something like depression?”

In the 1990s, the dominant message about depression was that it’s a chemical imbalance in the brain, likely involving the neurotransmitter serotonin. That view went hand-in-hand with the idea that depression is largely outside of our personal control.

Despite the lack of consistent evidence that depressed people have lower serotonin than people who aren’t depressed, the idea quickly became widely accepted among the public.

About ten years ago, Dr. Kneeland began to wonder whether the chemical imbalance view could actually make depression worse. Perhaps it gives patients the mindset that depression is beyond their control—and thus robs them of the cognitive strategies that might turn it around.

Putting the Mindset-Depression Connection to the Test

Evidence already indicated that there was a correlation between more fixed emotion beliefs and depression. But Kneeland wondered: Does depression make people’s beliefs about their emotions more fixed? Or are people who have fixed beliefs about their emotions more likely to get depressed—or stay depressed?

In one study (Kneeland and Dovidio 2020), she tracked a group of people at high risk for depression: first-year college students. Those who started the semester with more malleable views of emotion had fewer symptoms of depression near the end of it than those who started out with more fixed views.

In another study (Kneeland and Simpson 2022), she worked directly with people who have some experience of depression. Half of the group read a short article about how emotions are malleable; the other half read an article on an unrelated subject. Then everybody wrote a short essay about something bad that happened to them.

Those who received the message that emotions are malleable coped better. They used significantly more cognitive reappraisal, and their bad mood lifted more quickly. “They still get upset,” Kneeland told me, “but they come out of it faster when they’ve gotten the message that emotions can change, that your emotions are under your control.”

Kneeland thinks more fixed beliefs keep people stuck. Depression is, in part, a matter of getting stuck in low moods. It seems plausible that changing your beliefs about emotion might help with depression itself.

New Findings Highlight the Problem with the Chemical Imbalance Story

When we tell people that their depression stems from a chemical imbalance, are we inadvertently giving them the wrong mindset? Kneeland teamed up with Hans Schroder, a psychologist in the psychiatry department at the University of Michigan, to find out.

In a study published this year in Cognition and Emotion, they recruited nearly 300 people and split them into two groups. Both groups read about a hypothetical patient, Alex, whose depression was caused by an “overactive amygdala,” and both groups were shown a brain scan.

The only difference was the framing. The first group was told that Alex’s amygdala “is not doing its job,” and that something is wrong with her brain. The second group was told that her amygdala “is doing its job,” by signaling that something in Alex’s life is wrong. Her depression, in other words, is a helpful signal.

The first group thought Alex’s depression would last longer, that she had less control over it, and that she would need long-term treatment. The second group thought that she had a better chance of recovering, that she had more personal control over her depression, and that she probably wouldn’t need long-term treatment.

Mindset is not a cure-all, of course. Kneeland emphasized that there may be some conditions in which more malleable beliefs about emotions might actually leave you worse off—perhaps those with a stronger biological basis, such as bipolar disorder or schizophrenia.

The belief that emotions can change might also tip into “I should be able to change my emotions, and I’m failing to,” which could feed depression or anxiety. “A lot of that is an open empirical question about context,” she said.

The Practical Lesson: Seeing Depression as a Signal

The work of Kneeland, Schroder, and others leads me to think that seeing depression as a functional signal, not a malfunction, can help alleviate it in more ways than one.

Not only does it lead us to try to find the source of our depression—what depression is trying to tell us about our lives. It also shifts our beliefs about emotions toward the malleable end of the scale, and thus leads us to adopt exactly the kinds of cognitive strategies that are most helpful for working through it.

A version of this post appears on my Substack.

item.title: Our Slow Development Is Key to Human Uniqueness
item.description:
Neuroplasticity

Our Slow Development Is Key to Human Uniqueness

Humans are born most incomplete. And this is key to our unique strengths.

Posted October 22, 2026

Key points
  • Human newborns come into the world “incomplete,” more vulnerable at birth than other animal species.
  • Our “nature” is our ability to be shaped by our respective environments (e.g., our “nurture”).
  • The mechanism behind this is neuroplasticity: The young brain is malleable, shaped by early experiences.

The baby giraffe, weighing as much as 150 lbs, can stand and walk within the first hour of its life. The baby pig can start walking just minutes after birth. The baby iguana? Moments after hatching, it can leap into a full-out sprint to avoid predators.

The abilities of young animals can be awe-inspiring. How do the skills of the young human stack up?

If you've spent any time around human newborns, you'll be hugely underwhelmed. It's a lot of crying, a lot of diaper changes, and very little resemblance to the abilities of adult humans. They can barely lift their own heads, let alone walk.

Human babies are born most incomplete
Source: Alex Hockett / Unsplash

Compared to other animals, human nature has some very humble beginnings.

But from this humble starting point eventually comes the incredible sophistication, talent, and mastery that defines the human condition. All human exceptionalism, in all of its richness and diversity, stems from the same modest starting point.

How do we get there? When we examine the question of human nature through the lens of neuroscience, a compelling picture emerges. It suggests that the often incredible abilities of adult humans are inextricably linked to this "incompleteness" at birth.

How does the developing brain ultimately take on these skills and abilities? And what can this neuroscientific perspective teach us about the essence of human nature?

Let's dive in.

Human Uniqueness in Our Development

The first thing to note is fairly obvious: Compared to newborns, who are all relatively similar, adult humans differ tremendously. We come to hold a range of incredibly specialized skills and aptitudes. Some become astronauts, while others become rappers, athletes, etc. Some speak Japanese, while others speak sign language, or English, or speak many languages. You get the idea.

This basic observation poses a difficult question: How can we ultimately come to take on such incredible specialization, when our starting place, as newborns, is so unspecialized?

This brings us front and center to the age-old debate in developmental neuroscience about nature versus nurture.

Humans are born most shapeable to their environment
Source: Isaac Quesada / Unsplash

On one extreme view, we're born as blank slates: everything we come to understand in this world, from emotions to concepts to language. The shape and growth of our bodies may be genetically determined, but the contents of our minds are not. Nothing is predetermined. Here, culture, experience, and socialization play a complete and deterministic role in cultivating our inner lives.

At the other end of the spectrum, it's all innate. The essential features of our adult self are already genetically specified at birth. This includes our abilities and aptitudes, intelligence, and personality. Even a predilection toward being a musician, as opposed to being an accountant or some other profession, is ultimately an element of our genetic endowment. In this view, development is merely the process where these inborn features are polished and expressed.

While most neuroscientists and developmental psychologists will agree that the answer lies somewhere in between, the debate—especially about contentious topics like intelligence—rages on.

However, from the perspective of human nature, these two forces may be much more complementary than the debate typically poses. To whatever extent that the environment can shape features of our adult selves (e.g., nurture), it's fundamental nature of the human brain.

Let's unpack this.

Humans, as a species, didn't evolve many specific traits or tendencies. Unlike the Iguana, which can rely on pure, genetically imprinted instinct to sprint away from deadly predators moments after it has hatched, human beings have very few specific behaviors, pieces of information, and tendencies that are present at birth.

What we are born with is maximal flexibility. We're born with an openness, unlike any other in the animal kingdom, to be shaped by the specific features and experiences presented to us in our environment. Our specialization is the sheer capacity for learning and malleability.

In this view, the biggest contribution of our nature is that we are shaped so profoundly by our nurture.

The Pressures of Human Evolution

One interesting line of evidence for this view comes not from modern neuroscience but from anthropological investigations of ancient humans during a critical period in our evolution. Research spearheaded by Rick Potts of The Smithsonian's Human Origins Program finds that early humans faced unique and intense evolutionary pressures.

The geological record suggested that adaptability was very important for early humans
Source: Alex Hockett / Unsplash

Food resources were scarce and highly variable, the climate swung rapidly from season to season, and a wide range of large predators was an ever-present feature of life. The throughline of all of these challenges was variability in the environment: Early humans, during this time, could only afford to rest on their laurels for a short time. One season, they would need to catch fish to get by, but the next season or two, they'd need to hunt or forage for berries.

Coupled with the ever-changing weather and the dynamic threats predators face, there was no one lifestyle solution to settle into. Thus, forged through these environmental pressures, our distant ancestors slowly evolved this incredible capacity for change. Instead of developing a specific set of characteristics suited for a particular environment, these early humans evolved the capacity to adapt to whatever came their way.

The human brain evolved for flexibility, itself.

Human Uniqueness and Plasticity

Humans are born incomplete and, of any other creature, molded most significantly by their specific environment and set of experiences. But what precisely about the brain—especially the developing brain— makes human beings so open and uniquely adaptable? What is this natural feature of the human brain that provides this?

This comes down to neuroplasticity, which is the brain's incredible ability to be shaped by experiences and adapt following injury or ailment. It is the flexibility of the physical brain that enables it to change and evolve as we go through life.

Neuroplasticity is the basis for all human learning. Without this malleability, the brain would be unable to retain new information, create new memories, or improve our skills.

Human uniqueness comes down to our adaptability and sensitivity to our environment
Source: Jonathan Borba / Unsplash

While neuroplasticity persists throughout the lifetime, it is a much more robust feature of the young, developing brain. This is why learning, especially for implicit skills, is much easier early in life than later. Young children learn languages, for example, far better and more quickly than their adult counterparts, and they do so with little apparent effort.

By just two and a half years old, toddlers know up to 1,000 words in their native language, and can communicate substantial ideas. Moreover, children growing up in bilingual or multilingual environments will learn each language relatively easily. In contrast, if you've ever tried to learn a new language after your 20s, you know it's much more arduous.

Language learning is but one of many examples of developmental exceptionalism. Consider learning a new skill, such as a sport or instrument. These are undoubtedly much easier to master as a child than to try and pick up as an adult. The same 1,000 hours of learning are much more fruitful as a child than as an adult.

Our ability to learn by leaps and bounds as a young child is owed to the plasticity of the early, developing brain.

item.title: How Shame Gets in the Way of Anxiety Recovery
item.description:
Anxiety

How Shame Gets in the Way of Anxiety Recovery

Shame keeps us stuck rather than helping us find a way out of anxiety.

Posted October 22, 2026

Key points
  • Research indicates that shame and guilt are strongly associated with anxiety disorders.
  • Shame impedes the recovery process and keeps anxious individuals from coping adaptively.
  • A general reframing of anxiety as part of the human experience can help change the shame narrative.

Shame—the feeling that we are somehow “bad” or broken—gets in the way of many facets of our lives, and one of these that I have both experienced personally and observed in my clinical practice is our ability to cope with and recover from anxiety. Anxiety, although commonly experienced and not necessarily indicative of a diagnosable mental disorder, can often feel like a problem we are suffering from in isolation, while those around us seem to function without any trouble whatsoever. The problem with this way of thinking is that it incorrectly positions anxiety as something that is shameful and embarrassing, and that indicates a personal failing.

The sheer prevalence of anxiety challenges the notion that it is a “rare” or “uncommon” condition, let alone one that should be viewed with shame. In fact, the latest statistics show that more than 30 percent of U.S. adults experience an anxiety disorder at some point in their lives (NAMI, 2024), while a 2024 survey revealed that nearly 20 percent of adults reported experiencing anxiety symptoms in the past two weeks (Terlizzi & Zablotsky, 2024). To frame anxiety as an outlying, neurotic condition is to ignore its omnipresence. Normalization of the experience of anxiety is vital to challenging the belief that it deserves to be treated with contempt.

Research Links Shame With Anxiety and Social Anxiety

Beyond the statistics that highlight anxiety’s prevalence, there are also numerous studies and scholarly articles linking anxiety to shame and indicating “a growing body of investigations showing that shame and guilt are important features of various psychological problems including anxiety disorders” (Candea & Szentagotai, 2018). A 2021 meta-analysis found that, in “thirty-seven articles included in the current review [which] empirically examined the direct association between shame and [anxiety],…35 reported significant positive correlations between shame and social anxiety” (Swee et al., 2021). The link between anxiety and shame cannot be denied.

But what does this link mean in terms of anxiety coping and recovery? Shame, as defined by June Tangney, a distinguished university professor in the psychology department at George Mason University, is when “we feel bad about ourselves. We are fundamentally flawed because we did something. It reflects on who we are as a person. I’m a bad person for having done that” (APA.org, 2023). Now consider the harshness of this type of self-assessment: I felt anxious; therefore, I am fundamentally flawed and am a bad person. This is hardly motivating language for someone who is trying to cope with a problem or navigate a challenge. Yet, it is the way many anxious people (myself included) speak to themselves. It is common to assign self-negative assessments to our experience with anxiety, which often manifest in the form of shame and humiliation.

The irony here is that one of the main things we look for when we are anxious is reassurance; for example, we long to be assured that we are safe and that all is well when we feel an intense wave of worry or panic. Yet, the inner language of shame is anything but reassuring. Rather, it perpetuates an inner narrative of being, as Tangney describes, “flawed” and “bad.” It is difficult to find reassurance in that type of message. In addition to not being reassuring, shame also keeps us stuck and works against motivation to change. Imagine wanting to learn a new skill but each time you attempt it, you say to yourself, “I am so bad at this.” The chances of sharpening that skill are slim in the face of such self-recrimination. In essence, shame does nothing for motivation or ability to move forward.

Reframing Anxiety as a Shared Human Experience Reduces Shame

So, is it as simple as just speaking to ourselves more kindly? Yes and no—while a little positive, supportive self-talk would go a long way toward helping feel less anxiety-based shame, it is not that simple. A larger reframing, redefining, and redescription of the experience of anxiety is necessary. Rather than framing it as “disordered,” “dramatic,” “histrionic,” or “irrational,” anxiety can be seen as an uncomfortable yet commonly experienced phenomenon that affects many individuals. If we can accept anxiety as a part of the human experience, we can fight the unhelpful shame narrative. After all, if shame makes us feel alone, then acceptance can cultivate commonality and mutuality, which can combat the idea that anxiety is an experience that should be hidden from the world and dealt with in shameful solitude.

My own experience, as well as my years of clinical work with individuals experiencing anxiety and panic, reminds me daily that anxiety, when viewed as pathological and purely diagnostic, brings feelings of shame and humiliation, isolates those experiencing it, and paints a picture of the person as broken. When, however, anxiety is viewed as a normal, albeit uncomfortable and challenging, part of being human, shame reduces, and real healing begins.

item.title: "Digger" and the Problem of Failed Satire
item.description:
Media

"Digger" and the Problem of Failed Satire

Satire is highly effective when it works—but it can be deadly when it doesn't.

Posted October 22, 2026

Key points
  • Satirists employ irony, exaggeration, and humor to ridicule their targets.
  • Audiences may fail to appreciate the satiric intentions of authors and filmmakers.
  • "Digger" is the latest in a long line of satiric misfires.
Comedy is hard, and satire is even harder
Source: Grok /xAI

Few actors are a more reliable box-office draws than Tom Cruise: Worldwide, his films have grossed over $13 billion during his career. Director Alejandro Iñárritu has twice been honored with the Academy Award for best director (for "Birdman" and "The Revenant"). A movie that combines their formidable talents seems like a sure-fire winner—at least on paper.

But things didn’t turn out that way. In early October, "Digger" was released theatrically, and it generated domestic ticket sales of just $8 million over its opening weekend.

After three weekends, the film has earned just $42 million worldwide—far short of the revenue needed to recoup its production and marketing costs (estimated at $300 to $350 million in total). It is being widely described as a box-office bomb.

What went wrong? In hindsight, it’s easy to point fingers. Perhaps it was the film’s idiosyncratic trailer, or maybe a confusing marketing campaign was to blame.

But another reason for its underperformance may be the film’s genre. Digger is a satirical black comedy, and satire is notoriously difficult to execute—or even to be recognized as such.

Satirists have traditionally used tools like irony, exaggeration, and humor to lampoon their targets. "The Simpsons" would be a good example of this. But since it is a cartoon, we naturally expect outrageousness in the service of its social commentary.

Tom Cruise, on the other hand, is primarily known for his action movies, so theatergoers may not have been expecting a critique of corruption, greed, and environmental degradation.

Not What the Director Intended

But in failure, "Digger" has plenty of company. In 1997, Paul Verhoeven directed "Starship Troopers," which he conceived as a satire of fascism, militarism, and authoritarianism. Even though the film is full of over-the-top fascist elements, such as visual allusions to Nazi uniforms, mass rallies, and propaganda, many viewers enjoyed it as an action movie that celebrated military heroism—the exact opposite of the director’s intentions.

Similar misfires are not hard to find. David Fincher’s "Fight Club" (1999), for example, was intended by its director to be a critique of toxic masculinity and consumerism. Nevertheless, some audience members came away thinking that its main character was charismatic. Similar reactions were noted after the release of Oliver Stone’s "Wall Street" (1987) and Mary Harron’s "American Psycho" (2000): the satiric messages of these films were not always received by their viewers.

300 Years of Satire

As it happens, this month is witnessing not only the release of "Digger," but also the 300th anniversary of one of the most famous of all satires. On October 28, 1726, Jonathan Swift published Gulliver’s Travels, a work written to lampoon specific targets, such as King George I, Sir Robert Walpole, and the Royal Society.

Over time, however, these specific victims—so obvious to Swift’s original readership—have become unrecognizable. Today, the book is often viewed as a critique of human nature in general, or simply as a children’s adventure story. Time has filed away the sharp edges of Swift’s critique.

It seems that satiric works have always been fraught. A generation before Swift, a practitioner of the form named Daniel Defoe published The Shortest Way with the Dissenters (1702). Taking on the persona of a zealous High Church Anglican, Defoe proposed that dissenting clergy be hanged and their followers expelled from the country.

Defoe, however, was himself a Dissenter, and he was using satire to criticize England’s High Church extremists. His critique was so deadpan that some High Church officials failed to recognize the mockery. (When they did, Defoe was charged with seditious libel and imprisoned for half a year.)

A century later, Jane Austen satirized her society’s obsession with wealth and social status in Pride and Prejudice (1813), and the craze for Gothic novels in her Northanger Abbey (1817). But once again, the satire has become less sharp over time, and adaptations of her novels—in film and on television—have emphasized the elements of courtship and romance instead.

Is It Good to Be a Giver?

Or consider Shel Silverstein’s The Giving Tree (1964). It tells the story of a boy and his interactions with an apple tree. As a child, he enjoys the tree’s shade and climbing in its branches. But as he gets older, the boy takes advantage of the tree’s bounty—he picks its apples, then saws off its branches (so that he can build a house) and finally cuts it down (so that he can construct a boat).

After each of these depredations, the narrator claims that “the Tree was happy.” And at the end, the tree has nothing left to give but its stump as a place for the boy, now an old man, to sit and rest. Nevertheless, we are assured that “the Tree was happy.”

What was Silverstein’s intention? Because The Giving Tree is a picture book, many have assumed that it was intended for children. It can, however, be interpreted as having very adult themes. It’s been suggested that the story is an allegory for unconditional love, or the parent-child bond. And it can also be read as satire—a cautionary tale about codependent relationships, or a critique of our exploitation of the Earth’s resources.

It is this ambiguity that is the hallmark of satire—and an important reason why it is so often misinterpreted. "Digger" may have failed theatrically, but it would not be the first such work to miss its mark.

item.title: Savoring the Ordinary
item.description:
Attention

Savoring the Ordinary

How brief practices of “beginner’s mind” can enhance your life.

Posted October 22, 2026

Key points
  • Automatic pilot can lead us to ignore everyday sources of joy and awe.
  • Cultivating “beginner’s mind” and truly attend to the ordinary can help change this.
  • Adding brief savoring practices can enhance our well-being.
Source: Josh Bartok/ Used with Permission

By Lizabeth Roemer, Ph.D., and Josh Bartok, M.S

Author and cartoonist Sophie Lucido Johnson shared a post on Instagram, reminding people that “ordinary” birds like robins and house sparrows are actually extraordinary if you pay attention. She cautions viewers not to dismiss them with the phrase “It’s just a….” How often do we dismiss elements and moments of our lives in a similar way? We have written about other lessons for well-being that come from birding here and here. And Johnson provides yet another lesson in well-being from birding—the benefits of viewing the ordinary with fresh eyes and interest. What if we encounter the everyday not as “just another….” but as a luminous manifestation of itself?

Our minds’ ability to quickly recognize familiar stimuli allows us to preserve our attention for input that requires more cognitive resources. While this is adaptive, it can also lead us to overlook sights, sounds, tastes, smells, and sensations that bring with them a sense of joy, satisfaction, meaning, or connectedness. We might be so focused on preparing for a busy day that we fail to notice leaves turning, flowers blooming, birds chirping, or a stranger’s kindness during our commute.

We can similarly overlook “ordinary” actions we or others engage in, leading us to not appreciate the many small contributions we are each making to one another and the world. We may dismiss others’, or even our own, small acts of kindness or moments of connection as “It’s just a thank you note”; “It’s just allowing a car to merge”; or “It’s just taking out the trash.” In this way, we may miss moments of generosity or care that can enhance our experience, particularly when our attention is so easily drawn to acts of cruelty and harm.

One way to counter this natural inattentiveness to the mundane is to intentionally practice beginner’s mind, playfully meeting ordinary moments as if we had never experienced them before—with curiosity and wonder—rather than on automatic pilot or as “just” another iteration. Try these brief, simple practices and notice whether they enhance your life.

Notice your environment each morning

People often start their morning automatically engaging in a variety of activities that are needed before launching into their days. Spend 5-10 minutes of your morning bringing curiosity to typically mindless actions. What do you see around your house as you make your way through morning routines? Are there any sights that bring a sense of pleasure or pleasant recollection? What do you see out your window? Do you notice any sounds? Smells? What does your breakfast actually taste like?

Changing environments is an opportunity to notice

We regularly move from one place to another focused on where we’re going, rather than where we are—leading us to miss every step on the path to get there. Instead of focusing on your destination (or how long it’s taking to get there!), see if you can bring a fresh perspective to the journey as you make your way to work, your children’s school, or the grocery store. Notice the humans, animals, and plants you encounter along the path, including the birds that some people may regard as “just a pigeon” (or an ibis if you’re in Australia!).

Savoring activities

Repetition can lead us to become numb to activities that we initially chose because we enjoy or value them. Family movie nights can devolve into everyone distracted by their phones; favorite meals can be eaten mindlessly; and conversations can be interrupted by countless distractions. Removing distractions (like phones) and intentionally bringing a beginner's mind to these activities can enhance the satisfaction and reward you gain from them (Livingstone & Srivastava, 2012). We also may fail to notice and appreciate others’ routine activities as well—see if you can notice the mundane tasks someone near you does. Did someone clear the table, pay bills, make a meal, or do something else that enhances your life? Might there be some inward or outward gratitude you might want to express?

Paying attention to communication

We are inundated with emails, texts, and other forms of communication that lack personal connection and meaning. This can lead us to not appreciate when meaningful communications and connections do occur, such as a kind statement in an email, or a text from someone we haven’t seen in a while. Try practicing noticing these communications as they arise, and also intentionally providing brief, meaningful communication to others, as a way of countering the negative impact of information overload.

We invite you to turn your “It’s just a…” reactions into a moment of noticing and savoring, bringing appreciation, satisfaction, or meaning into your lives. Even the photo we include with this piece is an example of turning “It’s just a morning glory” into a moment of appreciation.

Josh Bartok is a contemplative photographer and life coach, and the author of two children’s books.

item.title: Touch Starvation: The Hidden Reason Why Couples Drift Apart
item.description:
Relationships

Touch Starvation: The Hidden Reason Why Couples Drift Apart

As affection fades, desire follows. How couples can reach for each other again.

Posted October 22, 2026

Key points
  • You can sleep next to someone every night and still feel touch starved.
  • When affectionate touch fades, many couples slip into a "roommate" or "teammate" dynamic.
  • Partners may avoid casual touch because they worry a hug will be read as an invitation for physical intimacy.

I see this all the time with long-term couples. They come into my Miami office because their sex life has slowed down or stopped completely. As the session begins, it becomes clear that the problem started outside the bedroom. Through the busy days, the hugs, the kisses, the hand on the back while passing in the kitchen quietly disappeared. No one deliberately decided to take a step back; touch just faded on its own.

This common phenomenon is referred to as touch starvation, and in long-term relationships, it’s more common than you may think.

Let’s Break It Down. What Is Touch Starvation?

"Touch starvation" is what happens when a couple goes too long without physical touch. You can sleep next to someone every night and still feel touch starved. It isn't necessarily about how physically close a couple is. It's about the type of touch.

Most couples can’t keep their hands off each other during the honeymoon phase. Those involuntary butterflies bring so many jitters and laughs that people just naturally touch. But the honeymoon phase typically only lasts 6 months to a year. As couples naturally evolve and build lives together, it’s common to see less touch, fewer giggles, and the impact of daily stresses on the relationship.

As life tests people, social obligations fill the calendar, work stress piles up, and kids become relationship distractions. Throughout the daily routine, emotional exhaustion sets in, and affectionate touch slowly falls off. Couples usually don't even notice it happening. It’s a behavioral pattern that slowly creeps into their everyday lives.

How It Affects a Relationship

When there is a lack of physical affection, a couple slowly falls into a "roommate" or "teammate" dynamic. They run a house and live well together, but the emotional and physical closeness subtly fades.

Over time, one or both people start to feel rejected, unwanted, or not desired by their partner. Once there is a lapse in physical touch, it is hard to get back to it. Reaching for your partner starts to feel awkward, or even risky.

This disconnect affects desire, too. When couples stop touching outside the bedroom, physical intimacy often decreases or stops altogether. Many of the couples who come to my practice for sexual issues are, at the root of it, suffering from touch starvation. And when it goes on long enough, couples start drifting apart in other aspects of the relationship as well.

This is more common than you may think, and the warning signs are often overlooked.

Where It Starts

Everyone is unique. No two people are going to have the exact same need for physical affection. This is one of the most common mismatches and forms of miscommunication I see in my practice.

Some people feel most connected through words, quality time, or acts of service, while their partner needs physical affection to feel close. Neither person is wrong.

There is another pattern I often see. One partner starts avoiding physical affection because they don't want a hug or a kiss to turn into an invitation for sex. So, they hold back on all touch. This triggers their partner to feel rejected, and the cycle continues. When couples can identify the negative cycles they have fallen into, say them out loud, and realize no one intentionally meant to cause the other hurt, it is often a huge relief for both.

How to Start Talking About It

Many couples avoid the conversations they believe will start a fight. At the time, they feel it is easier to push down the painful emotion and focus on the tasks at hand. But over time, these feelings pile up and will eventually cause resentment.

The only way to break these cycles is to bring them up and name the pattern you are noticing.

To have an effective conversation with your partner, there are a few things to consider. Schedule the conversation for an appropriate moment. Don’t bring it up in bed, never in the middle of an argument, and avoid springing it on them during stressful parts of the day. Choose a time when both of you are calm and can focus on the topic at hand.

Most couples will not agree on how much touch is enough and how much is too much. It’s OK to not agree with your partner all the time. Once each of you has shared your desired dose of physical affection, start negotiating. Meet in the middle. Find a common ground. The goal is for each person to feel desired, loved, and satisfied in their relationship. Couples also thrive with touch boundaries. Where some touch is just touch. For example, where a hug in the kitchen or a gentle caress on the back does not come with an expectation that leads to sex.

Start small and be consistent. Affection that comes back a little at a time tends to stick.

Signs to Watch for

The signs are subtle, and most couples miss them. You will most likely feel emotionally and physically distant before you ever notice the diminished hugs and kisses. Below are a few signs to keep on your radar.

  1. If you find yourself keeping score of who initiates hugs, kisses, or sex, this is a clear sign that something is off.
  2. If you notice yourself avoiding touch out of fear of rejection or fear that your partner will want more, this is a sign the relationship is in distress.
  3. If one partner starts seeking validation or affection outside of the relationship, this is a sign their needs are not being met inside it.

To avoid falling into the touch starvation trap, make a physical and emotional connection with your partner every day.

Tonight, try one small thing. Reach for your partner's hand.

item.title: What Really Keeps Couples From Having Sex
item.description:
Sex

What Really Keeps Couples From Having Sex

Research reveals why sex doesn't always happen, and why it matters.

Posted October 22, 2026

Key points
  • The single most common reason people cite for not having sex is that "It just didn't happen."
  • Sexual satisfaction is higher when couples attribute not having sex to shared circumstances.
  • Sexual satisfaction is lower when people attribute not having sex to a partner's lack of interest.
Source: Vitaly Gariev / Unsplash

Why do couples sometimes go days, weeks, or even longer without having sex? And when sex doesn't happen, do men and women tend to explain it differently?

While researchers have spent considerable time studying why people have sex, they've devoted far less attention to understanding why people don't. However, the reasons couples aren't having sex may tell us something important about their relationships.

In a study published in the Journal of Sexual Medicine, researchers followed couples over a 30-day period to explore reasons for not having sex, how they differed by gender, and how different reasons were associated with sexual desire, sexual satisfaction, and relationship satisfaction.

Why Couples Aren't Having Sex

In this study, researchers recruited 87 male-female couples who had been together for about nine years on average. Most participants were in their early 30s, identified as heterosexual (90 percent of women and 98.5 percent of men), and were from the United States (82 percent).

Each participant completed a five-minute survey each day for 30 days that inquired about their sex lives. On days participants reported not having sex, they were asked why sex didn't take place. They were given a list of options to choose from, as well as an open-ended “other” option in case none of those reasons applied. Participants could endorse multiple reasons, if applicable.

Interestingly, the most common explanation wasn't a lack of desire, exhaustion, or relationship conflict. More often than not, participants said, "It just didn't happen." This was true across genders. Men and women were also equally likely to say “We didn’t have time.”

There were no gender differences in the “other” category, either, where people referenced things like logistical issues (such as having houseguests), being sick, having relationship conflict, and being stressed.

However, some notable gender differences emerged when looking at other reasons for not having sex. For example, women were more likely than men to report reasons pertaining to their own interest in or feelings about sex, including “I didn’t want to”; “I wasn’t in the mood”; “I was too tired'; and “Sex is painful.”

By contrast, men were more likely than women to report reasons pertaining to their partner’s interest: “My partner didn’t want to”; “My partner wasn’t in the mood”; and “My partner was too tired.” Men were also more likely to report that “Children got in the way.”

Reasons for Not Having Sex and Relationship Satisfaction

Not all reasons for skipping sex have the same implications for couples' sexual and relationship well-being. In fact, one of the most interesting findings was that satisfaction varied depending on whether people attributed the absence of sex to themselves, their partner, or shared circumstances.

For men and women alike, sexual satisfaction was lower when their reasons for not having sex centered around their partner; however, satisfaction was higher when the reasons were joint (e.g., “it just didn’t happen”; “We didn’t have time”).

In other words, there may be an important difference between feeling that sex didn't happen because your partner wasn't interested and feeling that sex didn't happen because neither of you had the time or opportunity.

For men only, relationship satisfaction was lower when their reasons for not having sex were personal (e.g., “I wasn’t in the mood,” “I was too tired”). However, relationship satisfaction was higher when it was a joint decision. Reasons for not having sex were unrelated to women’s relationship satisfaction.

Lastly, for both men and women, reporting personal reasons for not having sex was linked to lower sexual desire on the same day, as well as the following day; desire was higher when other types of reasons were endorsed. Also, for men only, desire increased on days after they endorsed a partner-related reason for not having sex.

Of course, it's important to highlight that these findings are correlational. We can't conclude that particular reasons for not having sex cause changes in desire or satisfaction. For example, people who are already less sexually satisfied may be more likely to interpret a partner's lack of interest negatively.

Takeaways

One important conclusion here is that not having sex isn't necessarily a sign that something is wrong in a relationship. Sometimes sex just doesn't happen because life gets in the way, and when both partners view the absence of sex as the result of shared circumstances, that doesn't necessarily harm sexual satisfaction.

Further research is needed to explore whether reasons for not having sex are similar or different in LGBTQ+ relationships. In addition, future studies would do well to expand definitions of “sexual activity.” It’s possible that when some people avoid sex, they still engage in intimate physical contact with their partner, such as kissing or cuddling. To the extent that this happens, it may reduce any negative impacts on subsequent satisfaction and desire.

That said, a key takeaway here is that how often couples have sex isn't the sole metric of sexual satisfaction. It's also important to understand how couples navigate the times when sex doesn't happen. Two couples might have sex equally often but feel very differently about their intimate lives depending on whether they see periods without sex as a shared reality or a source of rejection and frustration.

item.title: Procrastination Isn't Laziness; It's an Alibi to Be Avoided
item.description:
Procrastination

Procrastination Isn't Laziness; It's an Alibi to Be Avoided

Putting things off protects your ego, but the consequences can destroy you.

Posted October 22, 2026

Key points
  • Procrastination is a self-protective strategy, not a time-management failure.
  • Delay is an excuse: If you fall short, you blame the strategy instead of your ability.
  • Lasting change requires revising your self-beliefs, not using AI or better planning software.
Source: Google Gemini/AI image generator

Every October, 20 million procrastinating Americans run up against a self-imposed deadline. October 15 is the tax-filing deadline for taxpayers who requested an extra six months to file their annual income tax returns with the Internal Revenue Service (Gore, 2026). Plenty of extension filers had perfectly good reasons to request more time. But if you spent the second week of October scrambling for a missing 1099 at midnight or frantically find yourself stumbling toward an important deadline, you probably don’t realize why this deferral tactic happens over and over.

Most advice on procrastination treats it as a scheduling problem. Experts tell you things like download an app, use an artificial intelligence (AI) agent to coordinate your schedule, set a timer, or break the task into smaller chunks. These strategies might work, but they treat symptoms, not the underlying cause of your productivity grief. Imagine if your doctor handed you painkillers for recurring headaches without asking when the headaches occurred; wouldn't you be suspicious? Eliminating procrastination requires the same root cause analysis.

What procrastination really is

Procrastination isn’t about laziness. It is intentional task deferral when deadlines matter, despite knowing the delay may hurt your performance, reputation, or peace of mind. The psychological costs of procrastination are real. Procrastination is consistently linked to lower-quality work (Kim & Seo, 2015), and in a large study following more than 3,500 Swedish university students, the researchers concluded that higher procrastination predicted lower mental health, poorer sleep, and more angst, even months later (Johansson et al., 2023). So why do smart, otherwise productive people keep procrastinating?

The success trap

Part of the answer is that procrastination often works just fine, or, at least, that’s what you believe. When you pull off a last-minute win, the habit is rewarded (neurologically) and becomes more likely next time. Students sometimes use deadline pressure as a motivator and even turn delay into a game, waiting until the last minute to test their own abilities (Schraw et al., 2007), but to the chagrin of these hopeful procrastinators, the evidence shows that deferral strategies do not actually improve performance. The feeling of efficiency was real. The actual efficiency was wishful thinking.

The scary truth: It is about self-worth

A deeper dive into the causes of procrastination reveals a pattern of self-doubt about one's competence and abilities (Covington, 1984). That sounds illogical, because delay makes failure more likely, not less. The contradiction disappears once you understand self-worth. Everyone wants to feel competent and to be seen by others as capable. We judge our competence not only by results but also by how we interpret the reasons why we achieved those results. Two people can earn identical outcomes and walk away with different conclusions. A first-time author who publishes a book feels validated; a veteran author with the same book may feel defeated because results don’t match prior achievement. Falling short of our own standards, especially after real effort, produces guilt, shame, and humiliation. Covington, creator of self-worth theory, showed why avoiding perceptions of incompetence is paramount to acknowledging any other personal limitation. Covington cautioned that “one’s first priority is to act in ways that minimize the implications of failure, namely, that one lacks ability” (1984). If we procrastinate and fail, we rationalize that it’s because of the delay, and not because of any personal shortcoming.

The perfect alibi

Procrastination is a mask. If you wait until the last minute and fail, you tell yourself, "If I had started earlier, this wouldn’t have happened." The failure belongs to the strategy, not to you. If you wait and succeed, your self-image actually increases because you imagine what you could have done with real effort. Either way, your ability is never in question because procrastination becomes a winning formula to avoid a loser mentality. Procrastination has cousins that serve the same purpose: setting impossibly high goals, setting goals so low they require no effort, defensive pessimism, and using a "wooden leg," which is a single excuse that explains away a lifetime of underachievement. All of them redirect attention away from the self and keep self-worth intact. We would much rather assess our shortcomings as a consequence of inept strategy than admit the reality of incompetence.

How to lose the mask

If procrastination protects self-worth, then the solution is to make self-worth less fragile. Try this three-step process:

  • First, be self-aware. Notice when you are rationalizing before you start. Ask yourself what a sub-par result will say about you. Recall times you started early and succeeded, and what made that possible.
  • Second, choose tasks you can complete with your current skills and get objective feedback on the results. A coach, mentor, or colleague is often better than self-assessment at connecting specific actions to specific outcomes.
  • Third, remember that perfection is a myth. This is the hardest step, because people resist acknowledging their weaknesses. Accept that obstacles and imperfect results are part of the learning process. Remember, adversity leads to growth, and the most successful individuals on the planet have all failed at one time or another (Hoffman, 2015).

The scary truth about procrastination is not that you are lazy. It is that you are protecting yourself from a verdict you fear. Once you stop needing the alibi, you can finally reach your productivity potential.

item.title: Jung in Azeroth: The Psychology of WoW Forever
item.description:
Play

Jung in Azeroth: The Psychology of WoW Forever

Archetypes, adventure, and play, through a Jungian lens.

Posted October 22, 2026

Key points
  • Play is one of the oldest ways psyche grows.
  • Gaming can expand and enrich your life or unconsciously replace it.
  • World of Warcraft’s classes, factions, and deaths mirror archetypal patterns.
Source: Photo by Sander Sammy on Unsplash

On November 4, Blizzard Entertainment releases World of Warcraft (WoW): Forever, a reimagining of the game’s original 2004 world. The announcement emotionally stirred something in me: a homesickness for a place that never existed, yet has always been real to the psyche.

So, I am going back to Azeroth, likely to the dismay of the Horde players I plan to turn into sheep through magical spells. Playing the beta, I’ve noticed how quickly my body remembers the slow walk through an enchanted forest at dusk, or how relaxing it is to hear the music shifting as I cross into a new zone.

In my practice, clients often mention gaming the way people confess a guilty pleasure. However, I love these conversations; what we choose to play, and how we play it, can tell us a great deal about what the human soul is reaching for.

Play is serious business for the psyche

Some of psychology’s greatest thinkers took play seriously, in theory and in practice. After his painful rupture with Freud, a disoriented Jung returned to a childhood game: building a small village of stones by the lake. That play, he later wrote, opened the door to the inner images that shaped his life’s work.

Other psychoanalysts from Freud to Winnicott have written about play as well; it may be one of the oldest formative experiences we share across cultures, and play itself can be a form of liberation.

Choosing a class is choosing an archetype

Jung described archetypes as forms without content: inherited patterns that shape how we perceive and respond, and that surface as images in myth, dream, and story. World of Warcraft's classes are almost a field guide to them.

  • Mage: the Magician, who studies hidden laws and channels power through secret arcane knowledge. (I almost always choose the mage; make of that what you will!)
  • Warrior: the Hero, whose deepest battle, Jung suggested, is freeing consciousness from the pull of the unconscious; fittingly, warriors draw power from rage.
  • Priest: the Healer, who can walk the path of Light or of Shadow; the game itself knows that these paths belong to the same person.
  • Rogue: the Trickster, a master of disguise who unsettles the persona and moves through shadow; Jung saw figures like this as both poisonous and medicinal.
  • Druid: the Shapeshifter, at home in bear, cat, and humanoid form; individuation and development as a process, never a finished shape.
  • Hunter: the one who travels the wilderness with an animal companion; instinct as ally rather than enemy.
  • Warlock: the one who makes pacts with demons, raising the oldest question about the shadow: integration or possession?
  • Shaman: the mediator between worlds, speaking with elements and spirits, much like Jung’s transcendent function.
  • Paladin: the holy grail knight, devoted to a search for wholeness, and always at risk of righteousness tipping into inflation.

Notice, too, that no one finishes a dungeon alone. A group needs someone to protect, someone to heal, and someone to strike. Psyche works in much the same way: differentiated parts, each limited on its own, and yet becoming whole only in relationship.

Why we go on adventures

Campbell called it the call to adventure: the moment the familiar world grows too small and something beckons from beyond its edge. Modern Western life offers few initiatory structures; we are rarely asked to leave home, face real danger, find companions, and return changed.

The original World of Warcraft offered a safe, structured version of exactly that. You begin small, often gathering herbs and chasing wolves near a village, then venture into more dangerous lands and discover you cannot go far alone. WoW Forever promises to keep that slow road, and I suspect the slowness is the point; psyche does not individuate on a deadline.

Dying and walking back

Having spent much of my career with grief and dying, I find the way World of Warcraft handles death quietly profound. When your character dies, you awaken as a spirit in a distant graveyard, in a world drained of colour. To return, you walk alone back to where you fell, or accept a Spirit Healer’s resurrection and come back weakened for a time.

It is one of the oldest human patterns: descent and return. Death here is a passage, and it must be walked. Many people I work with know this terrain well: the grey world after a loss, the long road back, and the weakness that lingers once you arrive.

The faction you didn't choose

Every player chooses a side: Alliance or Horde. The game even garbles the other faction’s speech, so you literally cannot understand them. It is hard to imagine a cleaner image of projection: What we refuse to recognize in ourselves, Jung taught, we meet outside ourselves as an adversary.

Players who eventually cross over factions may experience a small revelation: Orcs can have honour, and humans can have cruelty. This is a beginner’s taste of shadow work.

When the adventure stops being one

Excessive play can also become a place to hide. I have sat with people for whom the game had quietly replaced the life it once enriched. Jung distinguished passive fantasy, which carries us away, from active imagination, where we engage the images consciously and let them change us.

Is this expanding my life, or replacing it? In Campbell's telling, the hero's journey is not complete until the hero returns home with their boon. What has the game given you—courage, belonging, adventure, etc.—that wants to come home into your waking life?

An invitation

If you are returning to Azeroth this November or simply remembering it, you might sit with a few questions:

  • Which class or race do you return to repeatedly, and what quality does it carry that you may be growing toward?
  • Who is your "other faction"? What might they be carrying for you in your own shadow?
  • What adventure is your soul asking for outside the game?

Play is one of the oldest ways psyche finds its way forward. As for me, I'll be the mage handing out conjured bread, water, and teleports in Stormwind.

item.title: When a Parent Denies Your Abusive Childhood Experiences
item.description:
Adverse Childhood Experiences

When a Parent Denies Your Abusive Childhood Experiences

A political ad highlights the pain of having a parent deny childhood abuse.

Posted October 22, 2026

Key points
  • Few understand how painful it can be when someone who was part of our childhood disputes our memories of it.
  • A controversial political ad highlights the painful reality of having a parent deny experiences in childhood.
  • When a parent comes forward publicly to dispute your claims of abuse, it can be retraumatizing.

A recent political ad in Ohio’s 2026 gubernatorial race has sparked controversy after candidate Vivek Ramaswamy released a video featuring the estranged mother of his opponent, Dr. Amy Acton. In the ad, Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, calls her daughter a liar and disputes her account of her childhood, urging voters not to elect her as governor (Ohio Capital Journal, 2026).

The controversy is especially painful given Acton’s publicly documented family history. Acton has said she experienced sexual abuse by her stepfather as a child and that her mother failed to protect her. In 1978, when Acton was 12, her stepfather was arrested and indicted on charges involving the rape of a child. Acton and her brother were subsequently removed from their mother's custody, and the siblings have said they have been estranged from their mother since childhood. Her stepfather was never tried on those charges (WOSU Public Media, 2026).

While the ad has drawn criticism from people across the political spectrum, the situation raises a deeply personal question: What happens when someone who was part of our childhood disputes our experience of it? And what happens when that person publicly calls us a liar about our own experiences?

It is one thing to have someone disagree with you about an event you experienced as an adult. It is something else entirely when the person questioning your memory is someone who helped shape your earliest understanding of the world. Someone who was there. Someone who, in many cases, was supposed to protect you.

Source: Image by Alexa from Pixabay

Exploiting Childhood Trauma and Reinforcing Victim-Blaming

When a parent disputes their child's experience of childhood, the disagreement is rarely just about what happened. It can reach much deeper, touching the child's sense of self, their memories, and their ability to trust their own perceptions.

For many survivors, victim blaming continues long after childhood abuse has ended. They may have spent years trying to make sense of their experiences, perhaps through therapy, conversations with trusted people, or simply hoping the pain will dull with the passage of time. They may have reached a place where they can acknowledge what happened and begin to heal from it.

Then, a parent disputes their account, and suddenly they find themselves revisiting questions they thought they had already answered. And when this happens publicly, it can be retraumatizing. Instead of being able to process their experiences on their own terms, they may feel pressured to defend their memories, explain things, or prove that the abuse happened to them was real. Not only is this victim-blaming, but it is retraumatizing.

And when the person denying your experience is someone who was supposed to protect you, the pain can go far beyond feeling misunderstood; it can feel like a rejection of your reality all over again.

When Childhood Trauma Becomes Public, Victim Blaming Follows

When a parent comes forward publicly to dispute your claims of abuse, it can be retraumatizing. It can reopen wounds you may have spent years trying to heal, forcing you to revisit painful memories. And survivors then have to watch others weigh in on an experience they know very little about.

Part of what makes this so painful is that we often want our parents to understand us. Even as adults, we may hope that one day they will acknowledge what we experienced, recognize how their actions affected us, or, even just at minimum to simply listen without becoming defensive. We may hope that if we explain ourselves clearly enough, they will finally understand. So many survivors can relate to this hope. I can relate to this hope.

If you also know this pain, you are not alone in navigating this.

item.title: 3 Strong Signs Your Partner Has an Obsessive Personality
item.description:
Relationships

3 Strong Signs Your Partner Has an Obsessive Personality

An emotionally attuned partner can help one break their obsessive streak.

Posted October 22, 2026

Key points
  • When a person’s interests suddenly narrow down to a single preoccupation, it could be a sign of obsession.
  • Obsessive individuals might fixate on specific actions or words, replaying them in their minds and out loud.
  • Obsessive thoughts or behaviors may consume so much time and energy that personal health becomes secondary.
Source: Yogendra Singh / Pexels

Passion is a valued personality trait. We are inspired by people who wear passion on their sleeves, and we do our best to bring passion into our own endeavors. When it comes to love, having a passionate relationship is often viewed as the pinnacle of romantic experience.

One study found that “zest,” or the ability to approach situations with excitement and energy, is top on the list of helpful character strengths when approaching everyday challenges. Other research has found passion to have strong ties to life satisfaction.

However, psychologists will tell you there’s a fine line between passion and obsession. For one, they both qualify as “hot” emotional states—characterized by intense emotions such as alertness, excitedness, and elation as opposed to “cool” emotions like relaxation, calm, and serenity. The same traits that lead someone to be the inspiring person who goes all in on the things they care about can, in certain cases, turn toward mania, rumination, insecurity, and impulsiveness.

Here are three things to keep an eye on if you fear your romantic partner or someone you care about might be acting obsessively, and what you can do about it.

1. Multiple Interests or Hobbies Dwindle to One Preoccupation

When a person’s range of interests suddenly narrows down to a single preoccupation, it could be a sign of obsessive behavior. Whether it's a hobby, activity, or even thoughts focused on one subject, the shift from versatility and breadth to narrow fixations may indicate an unhealthy level of obsession. This intense concentration might lead to neglect of other essential aspects of life.

To address this, you can encourage your partner to experiment with a broad range of activities and interests. Suggest revisiting abandoned hobbies or discovering new ones together. Open communication about the shift in focus is crucial. Understanding the reasons behind this narrowed attention can pave the way for finding a healthier balance.

2. They Become “Stuck” on One Thing You Did or Said

Obsessive individuals might fixate on specific actions or words, replaying them in their minds and out loud incessantly. This fixation could range from positive experiences to perceived slights or misunderstandings. This tendency to get “stuck” on certain aspects of their relationship may lead to persistent questioning, seeking reassurance, or even holding onto grudges.

To ease their stubborn stance, you can start an open dialogue about their feelings and try not to become upset by the focus of their obsessive thoughts, even if they are accusatory. If the fixation persists, seeking professional guidance from a therapist may help you and your partner.

3. Their Self-Care Routines Begin to Fall by the Wayside

When an individual becomes excessively focused on someone or something, their own well-being may take a backseat. This neglect is evident when self-care routines, such as proper nutrition, adequate sleep, and regular exercise, start to decline. Obsessive thoughts or behaviors may consume so much time and energy that maintaining personal health becomes secondary.

What you can do here is initiate conversations about self-care and well-being. Encourage them to maintain a balanced and healthy lifestyle. Support your partner in prioritizing self-care routines and find time for activities that promote their overall well-being. If needed, consider seeking professional help to address the underlying issues contributing to the neglect.

While passion is a vibrant and essential aspect of any relationship, recognizing when it tips into unhealthy obsession is crucial. Open communication, understanding, and a willingness to seek professional help can be instrumental in navigating these situations. Remember, fostering a healthy and balanced connection requires mutual respect and a shared commitment to emotional well-being.

A version of this post also appears on Forbes.com.

item.title: How Fear of Vulnerability Keeps Mental Illness Hidden
item.description:
Fear

How Fear of Vulnerability Keeps Mental Illness Hidden

Curiosity begins where 'I don’t know' usually ends.

Posted October 22, 2026

Key points
  • Fear of vulnerability can keep families silent about mental illness, even when they know the facts.
  • Patients and families alike shield themselves against vulnerability, and that armor keeps illness hidden.
  • Breaking the silence takes curiosity, which requires the very exposure that fear of vulnerability avoids.
Source: Christian Wasserfallen/Pexels

My brothers came to every one of my court appearances. They watched me at my worst as I was charged and punished for my actions while in a manic psychosis. But when I transferred to a state psychiatric hospital, they all but disappeared.

More than once, my mother has asked them why. Why did they stand by her through the criminal phase but remain silent through the slower, uglier work of recovery? I don’t know is the answer she hears. Her friends long offered a variation of the same refrain. On an early morning call last year, one close friend confessed: I don’t know enough about it, and I don’t want to say the wrong thing.

Since defense mechanisms, by definition, work outside our capacity to be aware of them, I don’t know may be an honest admission: we can struggle to see what’s stopping us from engaging, from asking a question that makes another feel seen. Stanley Cohen calls this implicatory denial: we accept the facts of what happened but not what they ask of us.

My brothers know the diagnosis and lived the horrors of its history, especially when my manic cruelty turned on their families. Still, I wonder why they turn away from what the knowledge would ask of them, or how it might implicate them. To be fair, I can’t read my brothers’ minds, and fear is not the only reason people keep their distance; anger, grief, and the urgencies of their own hectic lives surely play a part. But fear is a reason we rarely name.

They are not alone. For 10 years, when anyone asked what was wrong with me, I gave the same answer. While my I don’t know started in a brain that couldn’t see its own illness, theirs unfolded in selves reluctant to look. I suspect what united both was the same fear of vulnerability.

The Silence Surrounding Mental Illness

Vulnerability wears many masks. When psychiatry speaks of vulnerability, it typically means diathesis: one’s genetic and temperamental risk to develop a mental disorder. But in everyday terms, being vulnerable means fearing that others will see you as needy, wrong, scared, or unknowledgeable. And psychiatry is far less comfortable exploring this terrain of emotional exposure.

This fear of vulnerability perpetuates what my mother and I have started to call the fog and the silence of mental illness. The fog is anosognosia, a broken neurological instrument of self-knowledge rather than denial. It is an internal blindness that kept me from getting help for a decade. The silence, an external blindness, operates on two levels: the interpersonal silence of social stigma and the systemic silence of a fragmented mental health care system that never educated my family about my diagnosis or gave them a role in my care.

The mechanism that keeps mental illness hidden through the fog and the silence is not vulnerability but the defensive armor we put on to avoid it. Armor holds both blindnesses in place: it thickens the fog from within and amplifies the silence from without.

Carl Jung had a name for what you could call the fog’s accomplice: the persona, which is the face we present to the world. Mine was the intellectual hero, which was built on the conviction that I would rather be thought ambitious than exposed as afraid. When an AB in calculus contradicted the image of invulnerability fused to my intellectual identity, I vowed never again to place myself where anything could betray it.

What the persona can’t admit is relegated to what Jung called the shadow, which is where my bipolar illness found refuge, since being sick or weak had no place in the hero’s story. “When one’s conception of who one is gets stranded in time,” a leading psychologist of anosognosia, Xavier Amador, notes, “one can’t help ignoring or explaining away any evidence that contradicts it.” The illness removed my instrument of insight, and the persona ensured I would reject everyone else’s.

For its part, the interpersonal silence of stigma has its own engine: the fear of not knowing, which is how implicatory denial plays out in everyday life. It is what my mother’s friend meant when she said she didn’t want to say the wrong thing. Learning about bipolar disorder means first admitting you don’t know, and perhaps you don’t want to know, so silence feels safer than revealing it. Mental illness functions as our society’s collective shadow: the discomforting possibility we keep at a distance because it could happen to any of us.

My brothers’ armor did not form without cause. The threats I made were real, and they created real injuries: armor naturally forms around real wounds, which is why it can be so difficult to take off. Accepting that I have changed since then would require them to become vulnerable in the face of that harm, and open to the realization that their account of events is incomplete.

Source: Leonell Mendoza/Pexels

Moving Beyond Fragmented Care

The mental health care system has its own armor of specialization and siloing. While I was treated by psychiatrists, psychologists, neurologists, and social workers, no one practiced the kind of slow medicine that could see my case whole. Narrow clinical expertise is a structural way of never having to admit I don’t know. As Arthur Kleinman explains, patients need to know “that you, the caregiver, are also willing to reveal your own vulnerability.”

Recovery, for me, has been a story of embracing my vulnerability: owning both the illness and the harm, across a decade of my life, rather than exiling them. Jung described the task each of us faces as learning to “reconcile himself with his own nature—how he is to love the enemy in his own heart and call the wolf his brother.”

We can encourage the same reconciliation in those who love us. It begins with curiosity. My mother once did not know the word anosognosia, or much about bipolar disorder, or how to connect with a son who couldn’t hear her. She began by reading, asking questions, and speaking into the silence of ignorance. Where I don’t know closes the door, curiosity pries it open.

Curiosity requires exposure to the very vulnerability the silence conceals. For a brother, a friend, or a clinician, it may require them to confess ignorance, feel uncomfortable, risk being wrong, or modify an interpretation of the past where they found sanctuary. Curiosity can break the silence with the same three words this article opened on, followed by two more: I don’t know. Tell me.
